title: Arcadia Health x Redwood — Reference Program Kickoff
summary: Kickoff for Arcadia Health’s participation in Redwood’s customer reference program. Arcadia confirmed Dana Patel as primary spokesperson for reference calls and technical interviews, with Megan Cho as approver for compliance/security language. The group aligned on what can be published publicly (high-level architecture + quantified outcomes with caveats) vs what must remain private (exact traffic volumes, specific model names if tied to internal clinical workflows, any patient-data adjacent details). Redwood proposed an interview schedule (engineering + compliance + exec quote) and reviewed the approval workflow (draft review in Google Doc, then legal/compliance, then final sign-off). Metrics discussed for publication: latency p50/p95 improvements, error-rate reduction/timeouts, reliability/uptime windows, and deployment timeline for Private/VPC; cost metrics may be expressed as percentage ranges instead of exact $/1K tokens depending on Arcadia approval.
topics: Reference program expectations (public case study + reference calls)
What Arcadia will allow publicly (logo/quotes, architecture detail level)
Publishable metrics: latency, reliability, error rates, deployment timeline, cost framing
Reference call boundaries and scheduling windows
questions: Can Redwood name the deployment as 'VPC/Private' publicly, or should it be described as 'private network deployment'?
Are exact model names allowed in the case study, or should they be described generically (e.g., 'a 70B-class open model')?
Can we publish absolute p95 latency numbers, or only percent improvement and test conditions?
Is Arcadia comfortable with logo usage on the website and PDF, or should the first version be anonymized?
action_items: Ethan Wallace (Redwood) — Send interview agenda + question set and a one-page outline for the Arcadia case study draft (due 2025-05-22)
Markus Klein (Redwood) — Provide a metrics validation template + definition of measurement windows (p50/p95, sample size, traffic shape) (due 2025-05-23)
Dana Patel (Arcadia Health) — Confirm internal approvers list (Comms + Legal contact) and preferred review method (Google Doc vs PDF) (due 2025-05-24)
Megan Cho (Arcadia Health) — Share redlines/constraints for security language (what we can say about audit logs, key management, retention) (due 2025-05-27)
Avery Johnson (Redwood) — Send proposed reference-call routing + frequency expectations (max calls/month, scheduling windows) for approval (due 2025-05-22)
next_steps: Schedule 60-min technical interview with Dana + Eric (target week of May 27).
Schedule 30-min compliance/security language review with Megan (target week of May 27).
Redwood to draft a v1 narrative with placeholders for metrics; Arcadia to review within 7–10 business days.
Decide by early June whether the public version is named (Arcadia logo) or anonymized for first publish.
Confirm reference call guardrails: topics to avoid, whether Redwood SE attends, and a max cadence.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Arcadia Health x Redwood — Reference Program Kickoff
Date: May 20, 2025
Time: 4:00pm PT
Duration: 47 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Avery Johnson (Redwood Inference, AE)
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference, Solutions Engineering)
- Camila Reyes (Redwood Inference, VP Marketing)
- Ethan Wallace (Redwood Inference, Writer / Product Marketing)
- Dana Patel (Arcadia Health, Director Platform Engineering)
- Eric Ramirez (Arcadia Health, Eng Manager)
- Megan Cho (Arcadia Health, Compliance & Risk)


[00:00] Avery Johnson: Cool. I think we’re good. Dana, Megan, Eric — thanks for making the time. This is the reference program kickoff. The goal today is basically to confirm spokesperson and logistics, and then align on what we can and cannot say publicly.

[00:19] Dana Patel: Yep. Sounds good.

[00:21] Camila Reyes: Thanks for doing this. We’ll keep it pretty tactical.

[00:25] Avery Johnson: Quick intros? I’m Avery, I own the account on our side.

[00:29] Markus Klein: Markus — solutions engineering, I’ve been on the security review and the Private deployment track with you all.

[00:35] Ethan Wallace: Ethan — I’ll be the one doing the interviews and drafting the story.

[00:39] Camila Reyes: And Camila, marketing lead, I’ll be the approver on our side for publishing.

[00:44] Dana Patel: Great. Dana, platform engineering. Eric runs the data platform team that’s been integrating the inference endpoints.

[00:50] Eric Ramirez: Hey.

[00:51] Megan Cho: Megan, compliance and risk. I’m mostly here to make sure we don’t accidentally create a problem.

[00:58] Avery Johnson: Perfect. So first decision point: for reference calls and for the case study, who’s the official spokesperson? We usually ask for one primary technical person and optionally a business exec for a quote.

[01:12] Dana Patel: I can be primary. For reference calls, I’m okay to do them as long as we’re clear on boundaries. And for interviews, I can do the technical interview.

[01:22] Avery Johnson: Great.

[01:24] Dana Patel: For an exec quote… maybe later. We can see. Our VP might not want their name on it initially.

[01:33] Camila Reyes: That’s totally fine. We can do a technical-forward story with one quote, or even no quote in v1.

[01:40] Ethan Wallace: Yep, we can write it without needing an executive if that’s a blocker.

[01:45] Avery Johnson: Second piece is approval workflow. Megan, you had mentioned on the security call that anything public needs a couple layers.

[01:53] Megan Cho: Yes. Minimum is me plus our comms team. If there’s any mention of, like, “healthcare” specifics or regulated workflows, legal might want to glance as well. We can’t have anything that implies PHI is being processed, even if it’s not.

[02:11] Markus Klein: Understood. We can be very explicit that the deployment is in your VPC and that Redwood does not store prompts/responses beyond configured retention, but we will not talk about patient data or clinical systems. We can keep it about platform and compliance requirements.

[02:25] Megan Cho: Exactly. Also, no screenshots that show internal dashboards or identifiers. Even a screenshot of a latency chart could have account IDs in the URL.

[02:36] Ethan Wallace: Totally. We can recreate charts in design if needed, or just use numbers in text.

[02:43] Avery Johnson: On the mechanics: we typically draft in a Google Doc, share with Dana as the point person, then you route it internally. Is that okay, or do you need PDF only?

[02:55] Dana Patel: Google Doc is fine as long as it’s view/comment, not editable by everyone. We can handle versioning.

[03:02] Megan Cho: And please keep a changelog. It helps if comms sees what changed from v1 to v2.

[03:08] Ethan Wallace: We can do that. We already have an internal comments log; we can export a change summary for you too.

[03:14] Camila Reyes: Approval timing wise, what’s realistic? We’re trying to publish in June or early July.

[03:22] Dana Patel: If it’s a clean doc and not too many surprises, 7 to 10 business days per round. But if legal gets involved, it can stretch.

[03:33] Avery Johnson: That matches what we’ve seen.

[03:36] Markus Klein: Maybe we should talk about content boundaries now so the first draft is clean.

[03:41] Ethan Wallace: Yeah. Dana, what level of architecture detail are you comfortable with? For example: “Requests route through customer VPC, private subnets, audit logs exported” — stuff like that.

[03:54] Dana Patel: High-level is okay. Like, “VPC deployment,” “customer-managed keys,” “audit logs exported to our SIEM,” that sort of thing. But we don’t want to publish network diagrams with CIDR ranges, cloud account names, regions, any of that.

[04:10] Megan Cho: Also avoid saying which SIEM vendor or exact retention period if it’s tied to policy.

[04:16] Markus Klein: Got it. We can say “integrates with customer SIEM” and “supports audit log export,” without specifics.

[04:24] Ethan Wallace: And model names? Sometimes case studies mention the specific open model families.

[04:30] Dana Patel: I’d rather keep it generic. “Open-weight LLMs” is okay. But not “we use Model X for this internal program.” That gets sensitive quickly.

[04:41] Eric Ramirez: Yeah, especially if people infer what we’re doing. We can say “summarization and document QA” at a high level, but not the specific domain.

[04:51] Camila Reyes: That’s fine. We can anchor the story on: regulated environment, private deployment, reliability, and predictable latency.

[05:00] Avery Johnson: Next: the reference call part. The program asks for scheduled reference calls with qualified prospects. We control routing on our side and we try to minimize burden — like max one or two calls per month.

[05:14] Dana Patel: One a month is safer. Two only if they’re very similar and we can do a combined one.

[05:21] Avery Johnson: Okay, one per month target with flexibility. We’ll also do a prep doc every time: who the prospect is, what they care about, and what topics to avoid.

[05:32] Dana Patel: Good. And I want Redwood to be on the call with me. I don’t want to get dragged into roadmap or pricing questions.

[05:40] Avery Johnson: Absolutely. Standard is AE + SE attend, and we’ll redirect anything commercial.

[05:46] Markus Klein: And we’ll align ahead of time on “do not answer” topics.

[05:51] Megan Cho: Also, no security attestations beyond what’s in your official reports. Like, don’t say “HIPAA compliant” unless you have a formal position.

[06:01] Camila Reyes: Totally. We avoid that language.

[06:04] Ethan Wallace: We’ll keep claims factual and tied to what you can validate.

[06:09] Avery Johnson: Okay. Metrics. For public case studies we try to include at least two quantified outcomes. The draft outline we had was like: latency improvement, reliability (timeouts/errors), and deployment speed.

[06:22] Dana Patel: Latency is fine if it’s contextual. Like “p95 improved by X% under our benchmark” with conditions.

[06:31] Eric Ramirez: Yeah, if you include the caveat: prompt sizes, concurrency, and that it’s within our VPC.

[06:38] Markus Klein: We can write it as “In Arcadia’s benchmark window (N days, replayed traffic, target context length), p95 decreased from A to B.” But if A and B are too sensitive, we can do percent only.

[06:54] Megan Cho: I prefer percent. Absolute numbers can become a contract expectation for other people.

[07:01] Camila Reyes: That’s a common request. Percent is okay.

[07:05] Ethan Wallace: What about reliability? We’ve talked previously about streaming stability and reducing 429s/timeouts.

[07:12] Eric Ramirez: We can talk about error rate reduction, again as percent, and maybe a statement like “reduced timeouts during peak.”

[07:23] Dana Patel: And also the operational thing — audit logs, key management, and being able to pass security review faster. That’s a real outcome even if it’s not a number.

[07:34] Markus Klein: We can quantify it as “security review completed in X weeks” if that’s okay.

[07:40] Megan Cho: Time-to-approval is okay as long as it’s phrased carefully. Like, “Arcadia completed its internal review in ~6 weeks” not “Redwood guarantees 6-week security approvals.”

[07:52] Ethan Wallace: Yep, we’ll phrase it as your experience.

[07:56] Avery Johnson: Cost is the other one. Do you want to include cost-per-1k tokens or anything?

[08:03] Dana Patel: Not publicly. Internally we track it, but I don’t want to publish our costs.

[08:09] Camila Reyes: Understood. Sometimes we can say “reduced inference unit costs by ~X%” without dollars.

[08:16] Megan Cho: Maybe. But even that could be sensitive. Let’s see the draft.

[08:21] Ethan Wallace: We can leave cost as optional and focus on performance and compliance.

[08:26] Markus Klein: Another metric could be “uptime” or “availability.” But again, it needs to be consistent with SLA language.

[08:33] Avery Johnson: Yeah, we won’t claim anything beyond what we provide. Dana, would you be okay saying “achieved stable production with no Sev-1 incidents in X days” or is that too much?

[08:45] Dana Patel: Too much. Also because it tempts fate.

[08:48] (laughter)

[08:50] Dana Patel: We can say “improved stability” and maybe “reduced incidents related to inference timeouts” but not “zero.”

[08:57] Ethan Wallace: Makes sense.

[09:00] Camila Reyes: On the public vs gated question — are you comfortable being named? Logo, company name, all that.

[09:08] Megan Cho: I’m not ready to commit today. Our comms team is cautious. Potentially we start anonymized, and later we convert to named.

[09:19] Dana Patel: Yeah, I think that’s the path. We can approve a story that says “Large healthcare provider” or something.

[09:26] Avery Johnson: That still helps, and it unblocks us. For reference calls, those are 1:1 so we can disclose your name there with NDA on the prospect side.

[09:37] Megan Cho: Exactly. Reference calls are easier because we can require an NDA and we can be more direct.

[09:44] Camila Reyes: Okay, we’ll plan for anonymized public case study initially, with an option to name later.

[09:50] Ethan Wallace: Just to confirm: even anonymized, can we state it’s a VPC/private deployment?

[09:56] Megan Cho: Yes, “private network deployment” or “VPC deployment” is okay. Don’t mention region.

[10:04] Markus Klein: And we’ll avoid details like which cloud.

[10:07] Dana Patel: Correct.

[10:10] Avery Johnson: Great. Scheduling. Ethan will do two interviews typically: one technical deep dive, one stakeholder quote. In this case maybe we do technical with Dana + Eric, and a compliance review with Megan.

[10:24] Ethan Wallace: I’d propose 60 minutes with Dana and Eric. Then 30 minutes with Megan to verify security language and what’s allowed. Then we can do async review.

[10:36] Dana Patel: Works.

[10:38] Megan Cho: Works as long as it’s not a “tell me everything about your controls” call. It should be about phrasing.

[10:44] Ethan Wallace: Exactly. It’s phrasing and what we can say publicly.

[10:48] Markus Klein: We can join the compliance phrasing call so we don’t accidentally misstate our product.

[10:53] Avery Johnson: Also, for reference calls: preferred windows? We’ve got prospects across time zones.

[11:00] Dana Patel: Tuesdays and Thursdays, 11 to 2 Pacific. Keep it to 30 minutes.

[11:07] Avery Johnson: Great. We’ll route within that.

[11:10] Camila Reyes: Just to level-set expectations: reference calls will be with qualified prospects only — typically enterprise teams evaluating Private deployments or regulated workloads.

[11:21] Dana Patel: That’s fine. I’m not doing “what is an LLM” calls.

[11:24] Avery Johnson: Totally.

[11:26] Ethan Wallace: Can we talk about the narrative arc so I don’t go off track? From my notes: you needed private network deployment, auditability, predictable latency, and a path to model version pinning and rollouts.

[11:41] Dana Patel: Yep. And we had issues with prior approaches. Like, with some managed services we couldn’t get the logging we needed, and with self-hosting it was too much ops overhead.

[11:52] Markus Klein: You can mention you evaluated “managed endpoints” and “self-hosted,” but maybe not name vendors?

[11:58] Megan Cho: Please don’t name vendors.

[12:00] Eric Ramirez: We can say “cloud managed endpoints” generically.

[12:04] Ethan Wallace: Got it.

[12:06] Camila Reyes: On Redwood’s side, we also need to ensure any claim maps to current product. So Markus will review technical accuracy.

[12:14] Markus Klein: Yeah, and we’ll add measurement notes: what p95 means, time window, replay, concurrency. That helps avoid misunderstandings.

[12:24] Avery Johnson: One more legal-ish item: We have a quote and logo release form. If we’re anonymized, it’s simpler. We can do a release that covers quotes with attribution like “Director of Platform Engineering.”

[12:39] Megan Cho: We still need a release if there’s any quote, even unattributed, because it’s still from us.

[12:45] Camila Reyes: Understood. We’ll route the release form once we have the final quotes.

[12:51] Ethan Wallace: For quotes, Dana, are you comfortable being quoted as “Director of Platform Engineering” without your name?

[12:57] Dana Patel: Yes. That’s fine.

[13:00] Avery Johnson: Great.

[13:02] Markus Klein: On metrics validation: we’ll want the source of truth. Like, where are latency numbers coming from? Redwood Console? Your internal dashboards? Both?

[13:12] Eric Ramirez: We have our own tracing in Datadog. We can share aggregated numbers, not raw logs.

[13:19] Markus Klein: Aggregated is perfect. If we can align on the same time window, we can say “measured via Arcadia APM + Redwood Console.”

[13:27] Megan Cho: Make sure nothing you publish could be reverse engineered into volume.

[13:32] Ethan Wallace: So no QPS, no monthly tokens.

[13:35] Megan Cho: Exactly.

[13:37] Avery Johnson: This might be a dumb question, but can we say “supports audit log export” and “customer-managed keys,” or does that trigger a deeper review?

[13:46] Megan Cho: It will trigger review, but it’s okay. It just needs to be accurate and not overly specific.

[13:52] Markus Klein: We’ll keep it accurate: KMS integration, audit log events, retention is configurable, etc.

[14:00] Dana Patel: Also mention the operational tooling. The dashboards helped us when we were tuning the load.

[14:06] Ethan Wallace: Redwood Console as a highlight.

[14:08] Dana Patel: Yeah.

[14:10] Avery Johnson: Cool. Let’s talk about the “reference readiness” baseline. We ask that customers are stable in production and have a clear story. I think you do.

[14:19] Dana Patel: We’re close. We’re not at 100% of our expected traffic yet, but we’re stable enough.

[14:27] Eric Ramirez: We’re still tuning some retry behavior and rate limits, but it’s mostly good.

[14:33] Markus Klein: That’s fine. For the case study we can scope it to “phase 1 deployment” and avoid claiming final scale.

[14:41] Camila Reyes: Exactly. We can publish a story about the initial deployment and then update later.

[14:47] Dana Patel: That’s better.

[14:50] Ethan Wallace: Okay, let me sanity-check a possible outcomes section:
- “Deployed private inference in Arcadia’s VPC with audit log export and customer-managed keys.”
- “Improved p95 latency by ~X% under benchmark conditions.”
- “Reduced inference-related timeouts by ~Y% during peak.”
Does that align?

[15:10] Dana Patel: Yes with caveats.

[15:12] Megan Cho: And keep “customer-managed keys” accurate. It’s “integrated with our KMS,” not “we hold the keys.”

[15:19] Markus Klein: Right, “integrated with customer KMS / key management.”

[15:23] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[15:25] Avery Johnson: On the reference calls, what are hard “no” topics? So we can brief prospects.

[15:31] Dana Patel: No patient data. No internal program names. No discussing our vendors. No roadmap commitments. No pricing.

[15:40] Megan Cho: Also no discussing incident details. Like, “we had an outage on this day.” Keep it general.

[15:47] Markus Klein: Understood.

[15:49] Avery Johnson: And topics you are comfortable with?

[15:52] Dana Patel: Why private deployment mattered, what the security review required, how we did benchmarking, and what the developer experience was like.

[16:03] Eric Ramirez: Also the batching/caching stuff, but not too deep.

[16:08] Markus Klein: We can keep it at “we configured caching/batching policies and saw measurable improvements,” not exact settings.

[16:16] Camila Reyes: That’s perfect.

[16:18] Ethan Wallace: I might ask in the interview about “before Redwood” baseline. Were you using any solution before?

[16:25] Dana Patel: We had a mix. Some internal prototypes with self-hosted, and some managed API tests. It wasn’t production-grade.

[16:34] Megan Cho: Again, no naming.

[16:36] Ethan Wallace: Yes.

[16:38] Avery Johnson: Great. If it helps, other prospects do ask “did you compare to Bedrock or Azure.” In a reference call you can say “we evaluated managed endpoints” and leave it there.

[16:50] Dana Patel: That’s fine.

[16:52] Markus Klein: One thing: If a prospect asks “what model are you using,” the safe answer is “open-weight models, selected based on internal requirements,” right?

[17:00] Dana Patel: Correct.

[17:02] Eric Ramirez: We can also say “we can’t share model selection details.”

[17:06] Avery Johnson: Perfect.

[17:09] Camila Reyes: Okay, logistics for the written piece: do you prefer we send a one-page outline first, before drafting full copy?

[17:18] Dana Patel: Yes. Outline first. That’ll save time.

[17:21] Megan Cho: Agree.

[17:23] Ethan Wallace: Great. I’ll send a one-pager with the sections: Challenge, Requirements, Architecture (high level), Implementation, Outcomes, and What we’d tell peers.

[17:36] Avery Johnson: Timeline: can we target outline by Thursday, then interviews next week?

[17:42] Dana Patel: Next week is okay. I’m out Friday.

[17:45] Avery Johnson: We’ll coordinate offline.

[17:47] Markus Klein: For metrics validation, Eric, can you share your definitions for p95? Sometimes folks compute it over different bins.

[17:55] Eric Ramirez: Yeah. We can share the query in Datadog. It’s p95 over 5-minute intervals, and then we take the max. We can align.

[18:06] Markus Klein: Great. That matters a lot.

[18:09] Ethan Wallace: And what window? Like, last 14 days, or a specific benchmark day?

[18:14] Eric Ramirez: Benchmark window was May 10 to May 17. But we can also use a more recent one if it’s stable.

[18:22] Dana Patel: Let’s stick to the benchmark week so it’s apples to apples.

[18:26] Markus Klein: Works.

[18:28] Megan Cho: If you publish a time window, keep it vague. “A one-week benchmark” not exact dates.

[18:35] Ethan Wallace: Good call.

[18:37] Avery Johnson: Another item: reference calls scheduling and intake. We’ll have our reps fill out a request form, and CS will approve. You’ll get a single email thread per request.

[18:50] Dana Patel: That’s fine as long as it’s not random Slack pings.

[18:53] Avery Johnson: We won’t do that.

[18:55] Camila Reyes: Okay, let’s do a quick run-through of the “what we want from you” in the program, just to be explicit:
1) One public case study (anonymized for now) with your review and approval.
2) Up to one reference call per month, 30 minutes, with Redwood attending.
That’s it.

[19:16] Dana Patel: Okay.

[19:18] Megan Cho: Works.

[19:19] Ethan Wallace: For the public doc, would you allow an architecture diagram that’s basically boxes: “Arcadia VPC,” “Redwood private control plane,” “KMS,” “SIEM,” “App services” — no details.

[19:34] Dana Patel: Possibly. But we have to see it.

[19:37] Megan Cho: If it’s that abstract, it’s probably fine.

[19:40] Camila Reyes: We can start without a diagram and add later if it’s easy.

[19:46] Ethan Wallace: Okay.

[19:48] Markus Klein: I’ll also note: we should be careful with words like “air-gapped.” You’re not air-gapped.

[19:54] Dana Patel: Correct. Do not say air-gapped.

[19:56] Markus Klein: Great.

[19:58] Avery Johnson: Anything else that’s a “no” word?

[20:02] Megan Cho: Don’t say “HIPAA compliant.” Don’t say “HITECH.” Don’t say “PHI.” If you need to indicate regulated environment, say “regulated” or “healthcare compliance requirements.”

[20:14] Ethan Wallace: Got it.

[20:16] Camila Reyes: We have standard language for that.

[20:19] Avery Johnson: Okay. I think we covered the core. I’ll open it up — any concerns about reference calls? Dana you mentioned boundaries.

[20:27] Dana Patel: Just… I want to be sure we’re not in a situation where someone surprises us with a security questionnaire live. That’s not a reference call.

[20:36] Avery Johnson: Completely agree. Reference calls are experience-sharing, not security due diligence. If someone needs a questionnaire, we route them to our security team.

[20:46] Markus Klein: And if they want deep technical architecture, we can do a separate SE-led call, but that’s not you.

[20:53] Dana Patel: Great.

[20:55] Ethan Wallace: For the interview, I’ll likely ask “why Redwood” and “what made you trust the platform.” Are there any internal phrases or approvals needed around that?

[21:05] Megan Cho: Just avoid “we endorse” language. Like, “best vendor ever.” Keep it as “met our requirements.”

[21:13] Dana Patel: Yeah, we can say “it met our compliance and performance needs.”

[21:18] Camila Reyes: Perfect.

[21:20] Avery Johnson: Alright, let’s recap next steps so we’re aligned.

[21:24] Avery Johnson: Ethan sends outline + agenda by Thursday. Markus sends metrics validation template. Dana confirms internal approvers and comms/legal contact. Megan shares constraints list and preferred phrasing. I’ll send the reference call process and max cadence in writing.

[21:44] Dana Patel: Yep.

[21:45] Megan Cho: Yep.

[21:46] Eric Ramirez: Works.

[21:48] Markus Klein: Sounds good.

[21:50] Camila Reyes: Thank you all.

[21:52] Avery Johnson: Thanks everyone.

[21:54] (Call continues with scheduling coordination)

[22:05] Avery Johnson: Dana, I’ll propose a couple slots for the technical interview. Next Tuesday 11am PT or Thursday 1pm PT.

[22:15] Dana Patel: Tuesday 11 works.

[22:18] Eric Ramirez: I can do Tuesday.

[22:20] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[22:22] Avery Johnson: Megan, for the compliance phrasing review, would Wednesday 12:30 PT work?

[22:28] Megan Cho: Wednesday is tight. Thursday morning maybe.

[22:33] Avery Johnson: Thursday 11:30 PT?

[22:35] Megan Cho: That works.

[22:37] Markus Klein: I’ll join that.

[22:39] Avery Johnson: Perfect.

[22:41] Camila Reyes: And after interviews, we’ll aim to send v1 draft within about a week.

[22:47] Dana Patel: Okay.

[22:48] Ethan Wallace: One more question: for the anonymized version, do you prefer “Arcadia Health” not mentioned at all, or can we use “Arcadia” internally and you approve the external anonymized name?

[22:59] Megan Cho: Externally, no Arcadia. Internally you can obviously use our name.

[23:05] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[23:07] Avery Johnson: Cool. I think that’s it. We’ll send calendar invites and follow-ups.

[23:13] Dana Patel: Thanks.

[23:14] Megan Cho: Thanks.

[23:15] Eric Ramirez: Thanks.

[23:16] Markus Klein: Thank you.

[23:18] Camila Reyes: Bye.

[23:20] Meeting ended (Fireflies continued recording a few minutes of silence)
